done: New server/src/worktreeSeed.ts: copies allowlisted untracked files (.env, config.env) from the main checkout into every new worktree, and clones warm directories (node_modules) instead of rebuilding them.
Two new project config keys, checked at the API trust boundary: worktree_seed (list of globs) and worktree_warm (list of {dir, lock} pairs). Both reject malformed shapes.
Wired into spawnAgent's prepareWorktree callback, after `worktree create` and BEFORE setup_argv, so a project's own setup hook finds the work already done and no-ops.
Clone invalidation: a warm directory is reused only while its lockfile content still matches the main checkout. A branch that changed its deps does the real install.

Loud where it matters: config that names something absent emits a worktree_seed_failed event. Quiet where the design is working: a genuinely changed lockfile, a file the worktree already owns, or no seed config at all.
Spawn-to-ready measurement on the `spawned` event: spawn_ms, seed_ms, setup_ms, plus the list of what was seeded and warmed.
Plain-English rendering for both new event types in web/src/lib/eventText.ts.
12 new tests (10 unit against a real temp filesystem, 2 driving a real spawnAgent) plus 4 new config-schema rejection cases.
decisions: worktree_warm takes explicit {dir, lock} pairs rather than guessing the lockfile from a file sitting next to the directory. Guessing only works for JavaScript projects, and a wrong guess silently hands an agent stale dependencies, which then fails somewhere unrelated and is expensive to trace back.

Warm directories are cloned with `cp -c` on macOS and `cp -R --reflink=auto` on Linux. On APFS and btrfs that is copy-on-write, so the copy is near-instant and costs no disk until something writes. Any other platform falls back to a real byte copy, which is correct but no faster than the install it replaces.
A misconfigured seed is loud but never fatal. It downgrades the spawn to the old slow path; failing the spawn outright would turn a config typo into a dead task.

A worktree_seed pattern that matched nothing is quiet if OTHER patterns matched, because projects legitimately list .env and .env.local together when only one exists. It is loud only when NOTHING in the allowlist matched, which means a config nobody is honouring.
Both keys are opt-in with no default. Hive's own project needs `worktree_warm` set on it for the win to be real (see followups); I did not write to the live project config from inside a task.

iffy.what: The clone is only fast on a copy-on-write filesystem.
iffy.why: This fleet is macOS on APFS, so the win is real here. On a filesystem without reflinks the fallback is a full byte copy of node_modules, which is not obviously faster than the `bun install` it replaces, and could be slower. Nothing measures which path was taken, so a machine silently on the slow path would look identical in the stats.

iffy.what: A large clone gets a 5-minute budget and a clean-up-on-failure, but the clean-up itself is unverified against a real interrupted copy.
iffy.why: If `cp` is killed part-way, the code removes the partial directory and retries with the filesystem fallback. That path is unit-tested with a stub that fails immediately, not with a copy interrupted mid-flight. A partial node_modules that survived would be worse than no warming, because the 'already present' guard would keep it on every later spawn.

iffy.what: The loud/quiet line is my judgment, not a stated requirement.
iffy.why: I made a missing lockfile and an unbuilt warm directory loud, and a genuinely changed lockfile quiet. If a project routinely spawns branches from a base whose node_modules is not built, it will see worktree_seed_failed on every spawn, and repeated noise is how people learn to ignore an event.

testing: Full suite: 1983 pass, 0 fail across 146 files. tsc --noEmit clean.
10 unit tests in server/test/worktree-seed.test.ts run against a real temp filesystem, so the copy and the clone actually happen rather than being asserted against a stub.

server/test/worktree-warm-spawn.test.ts drives a real spawnAgent and asserts the ORDERING claim directly: it records what the filesystem looked like at the moment setup_argv ran, and both the seeded .env and the warmed node_modules are already there. A seed that ran after setup_argv would be worthless, so this is the test that matters most.
The loud/quiet split is pinned by name in the tests, so a later change that turns a quiet skip loud (or the reverse) fails.

One test caught a real mistake in itself: the first version stubbed `cp` to return success without copying, so the warm assertion passed while nothing was warmed. The test now shells out to the real `cp`.
followups: Hive's own project config needs the keys set for this to do anything: worktree_warm = [{dir: node_modules, lock: bun.lock}, {dir: web/node_modules, lock: web/bun.lock}]. Worth doing, because this worktree had 16 tests failing purely because web/node_modules was never installed.
Nothing records whether a clone was copy-on-write or a full byte copy. If warm worktrees ever run on a non-APFS machine, the stats would not show the difference.

understanding.background: When hive starts an agent on a task, it makes a fresh git worktree for it. Git only puts tracked files there, so two things are always missing. First, the config files an app needs to run, like .env, which are deliberately kept out of git. Second, the installed dependency folder, node_modules, which has to be rebuilt from scratch. Both of those already sit in the main checkout on the same disk. Every orchestration tool in this space has the same complaint, and for Conductor it is the top one.
understanding.scope: The spawn path only. It adds one new file, two new opt-in project settings, and some timing numbers on an event. It changes nothing about how agents work, how code is reviewed, or how anything merges. With no settings turned on, spawning behaves exactly as it does today.
understanding.essence: Copy the missing config files and reuse the already-built dependency folder from the main checkout, before the project's own setup step runs, so that setup step finds nothing left to do. Reuse the dependency folder only while its lockfile still matches, because a matching lockfile is proof the dependencies did not change.
walkthrough: A task is dispatched and hive asks herdr to create the worktree, as it always has.
Immediately after, and before the project's setup command runs, the new seeding step looks at two project settings.
For each pattern in worktree_seed, it finds matching files in the main checkout and copies them across. A file the worktree already has is never overwritten.

For each entry in worktree_warm, it compares the named lockfile in the main checkout against the same lockfile in the new worktree. Same contents means the dependencies are unchanged, so the folder is cloned across. Different contents means the branch changed its dependencies, so it is left alone and gets a real install.
The project's setup command then runs as usual. Because node_modules is already there, hive's own setup script sees it and does nothing.
Two records are written: one listing what was copied, reused, and skipped, and, only if the settings named something that could not be found, a second one flagged as a failure.
The spawn event gets three timings so the saving is visible later rather than needing a stopwatch.
affected_areas: server/src/api.ts (the spawnAgent prepareWorktree callback and the spawned event payload)
web/src/lib/eventText.ts (plain-English text for the two new event types)
understanding.risk_assessment: Low, and mostly bounded by being opt-in. A project that sets neither key gets today's behaviour exactly. The sharpest risk is reusing a dependency folder that should not have been reused, which would give an agent dependencies that do not match its branch. The lockfile comparison is what prevents that, and it compares file contents rather than timestamps, because a fresh worktree stamps every file with the current time. The second risk is overwriting something in the worktree, which is prevented by never writing to a path that already exists. Config-supplied paths are also held inside the worktree, though that is tidiness rather than a security boundary: project config already accepts the command line used to launch agents, so it is a far more powerful surface than a file path.
understanding.participate: The judgment call worth your attention is the loud versus quiet split, since you raised it directly. I made noisy the cases where the config names something that is not there: a lockfile that does not exist, a warm directory that was never built, and an allowlist where nothing at all matched. I left quiet the cases where the design is doing its job: a branch that genuinely changed its lockfile, a file the worktree already owns, and a project with no seed config at all. The one I am least sure about is the middle case, where a project lists two config files and only one exists. I kept that quiet on the grounds that .env plus .env.local is a normal pairing, but if you would rather every named-and-absent file be reported, that is a one-line change.

checks.question: A branch adds a new dependency, so its bun.lock is different from the one in the main checkout. What happens when hive spawns an agent on it?

options.label: It skips reusing node_modules and lets the normal install run, without flagging anything
It reuses node_modules anyway, and the agent works with the wrong dependencies
It reports a failure, because the lockfiles do not match
It refuses to start the agent until someone updates the main checkout

checks.explanation: A changed lockfile is the exact signal the rule exists to catch, so it is treated as normal and stays quiet. The branch does its own real install, which is correct and only costs time. Reporting it would fire on every legitimate dependency change and train people to ignore the report.

checks.question: A project's settings name bun.lock as the lockfile to check, but no file by that name exists. What does hive do?

options.label: It skips the reuse and writes a failure record, but still starts the agent normally
It skips the reuse silently, the same as any other reason for skipping
It stops the spawn so somebody has to fix the settings first
It reuses the folder anyway, since there is no lockfile saying otherwise

checks.explanation: This is settings pointing at a file nobody has, so the reuse can never work on any spawn. Staying silent would move the hidden failure from a wrong guess to a missing setting, with the same symptom: a worktree that looks ready and is not. It is reported, but it never stops the spawn, because a typo in settings should cost speed and not a whole task.

checks.question: Why does reusing the dependency folder cost almost nothing on the machines this fleet runs on?

options.label: The disk format supports copy-on-write, so the copy shares the original data until something changes it
The worktree points at the main checkout's folder through a shortcut, so there is only ever one copy
Only the parts of the folder the agent actually reads are ever fetched
The folder is compressed first, so much less data has to move

checks.explanation: On APFS and btrfs, a clone records that the new copy shares the original's data, so nothing is actually duplicated until one side is written to. That makes a large folder appear in milliseconds and take no extra disk. Option b describes a shared link, which was deliberately avoided: a worktree changing shared dependencies would corrupt the main checkout. On a disk format without this feature, the code falls back to a real copy, which is correct but not fast, and that limit is called out as an open concern.
